decision.conviction_status: Accused Valerbhai Deganbhai Vagh (A-1), Unadbhai Deganbhai Vagh (A-2), Bhimabhai Deganbhai Vagh (A-3), Unadbhai Bhagabhai Vagh (A-5), Bhagwanbhai Bhikabhai Vagh (A-7), Bhikabhai Jinabhai Vagh (A-8), Hasurbhai Bhikhabhai Vagh(A-11), Bhanabhai Bhikabhai Vagh (A-12), Patabhai @Aatabhai Bhikabhai Vagh (A-13) and Bhavabhai Jikarbhai Vagh (A-14) are convicted under section 326 read with 149 IPC.

issue.issue_text: Whether a finding of the commission of the offence under Section 326 read with Section 149 can be recorded against members of an unlawful assembly even if it is established that the offence under Section 302 was committed by one member of such assembly.

facts: An unlawful assembly of five or more persons was formed.
The common object of the assembly was not to commit murder, but to attack or "teach a lesson" to the victim.
During the incident, one member of the assembly committed murder, an offense punishable under Section 302 of the IPC.
The other members of the assembly participated in the attack using deadly weapons.
law: Section 149 of the IPC states that if an offense is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object of that assembly, or an offense that the members knew was likely to be committed, then every member of that assembly is guilty of that offense.

The court cited the settled legal principle ("res integra") that a conviction under Section 326 (voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons) read with Section 149 can be recorded against members of an unlawful assembly, even if one member is found to have committed murder (Section 302).
application: The Court determined that the common object of the unlawful assembly was not murder. This was inferred from the circumstances, such as the lack of previous enmity and the immediate cause of the altercation.

Therefore, the other members of the assembly could not be convicted for murder under Section 302 with the aid of Section 149, as they did not share the common object to kill, nor could they have known that murder was a likely outcome.
However, the court found that the common object to attack the victim was proven.

Considering the manner of the attack and the use of deadly weapons by the members, the court concluded that their actions fell under the offense of causing grievous hurt with dangerous weapons (Section 326) in prosecution of their common object.
Consequently, the other members of the assembly were held guilty under Section 326 read with Section 149.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that members of an unlawful assembly can be convicted for the offense of causing grievous hurt under Section 326 read with Section 149, even if one member of the assembly committed the more serious offense of murder under Section 302. This is because the shared 'common object' of the assembly may have been to cause grievous hurt, but not necessarily to commit murder.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 149 IPC becomes inapplicable in all situations where there is a cross case by the accused.

facts: The High Court had set aside the conviction of the accused under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the IPC.
One of the reasons for the High Court's decision was the existence of a cross case filed by the accused against the complainant.
However, the complainant and others had already been acquitted in that cross case before the High Court delivered its judgment.
law: The Supreme Court held that Section 149 IPC does not automatically become inapplicable in all situations just because a cross case has been filed by the accused.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had erred by failing to consider the outcome of the cross case.
The High Court should have taken note of the fact that the complainant had been acquitted in the cross case, which meant there was no pending case against them when the High Court made its decision.

By acquitting the accused based on the existence of a cross case without considering its resolution and without re-appreciating the evidence, the High Court caused a "flagrant miscarriage of justice."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, stating that the existence of a cross case does not automatically render Section 149 IPC inapplicable. The court ruled that the High Court should have considered the fact that the complainants had already been acquitted in the said cross case, and its failure to do so was a serious error.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a finding of the commission of the offence under Section 326 read with Section 149 can be recorded against members of an unlawful assembly even if it is established that the offence under Section 302 was committed by one member of such assembly.
appellant_arguments: The High Court committed a serious error in acquitting the Accused under Section 302 read with 149 IPC.
The High Court's finding that there was no unlawful assembly or previous concert to cause death was without reference to the facts of the case.
respondent_arguments: The complainant's party were the aggressors, which implies there was no unlawful assembly with a common object on the part of the accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 149 IPC becomes inapplicable in all situations where there is a cross case by the accused.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's core argument that the accused should be convicted under Section 149 IPC implies that the existence of a cross-case does not negate the formation of an unlawful assembly.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution suppressed the true facts, as evidenced by a cross-case (Crime No. I 35 of 1998) lodged by the accused.
The complainant's party were the aggressors in the fight.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A finding of the commission of the offence under Section 326 read with Section 149 can be recorded against members of an unlawful assembly even if it is established that the offence under Section 302 was committed by one member of such assembly.
obiter: The construction of this Section (149), that is, a construction which shall be at once reasonable grammatical, involves two difficulties, or at least two points which call for attentive consideration.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A finding of the commission of the offence under Section 326 read with Section 149 can be recorded against members of an unlawful assembly even if it is established that the offence under Section 302 was committed by one member of such assembly. The court determined that while the common object of the unlawful assembly was not to commit murder, it was proven to be to attack the opposing party with deadly weapons. Therefore, all members are constructively liable for the offence of causing grievous hurt, which was committed in prosecution of that common object.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the two-part test for constructive liability under Section 149 IPC, as articulated in Queen v. Sabid Ali. An offence by a member of an unlawful assembly makes all other members guilty if either: 1) The offence was committed 'in prosecution of the common object,' meaning it is immediately connected with that common object by virtue of the nature of the object itself; or 2) The offence was 'such as the members of that assembly knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object,' even if not directly connected by nature.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant lost their primary argument for a conviction under Section 302 read with 149 IPC because the court found that the common object of the unlawful assembly did not extend to committing murder. The murder was an act by an individual member that went beyond the shared intention of the group, which was limited to attacking and causing grievous bodily harm.
why_respondent_won: The respondents (accused) won in the sense that their acquittal for the charge of murder under Section 302 read with 149 IPC was effectively upheld. The court's reasoning was that the prosecution failed to establish that the common object of the assembly was to cause death, or that the members knew that death was a likely outcome in the prosecution of their common object to merely attack the other party.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning seeks to prevent an overly harsh application of Section 149 IPC by carefully distinguishing between an act committed 'during the prosecution' of a common object and one committed 'in prosecution' of it. This ensures that constructive liability is not automatically extended to the gravest offence committed by any single member, but is instead tied to the specific common object shared by the group or the offences they knew were likely to occur. This avoids mitigating the 'rigour of the Section' by limiting the definition of 'common object' but instead insists on a factual determination of whether the specific crime fell within the scope of that object.
